questions.stem: The Big Bang theory predicts that the early universe was extremely hot and dense. As the universe expanded, this heat should have cooled. What form of radiation is this leftover heat observed as today?

options.text: Visible light from distant stars
Gamma rays from the edge of the universe
Cosmic microwave background radiation at a temperature of about 2.7 K
Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun

questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation is the cooled remnant of the very hot early universe. As the universe expanded for 13.8 billion years, this radiation stretched from very short wavelengths to microwaves, corresponding to a temperature of about 2.7 K (-270.5 degrees Celsius). It is not visible light (A), gamma rays (B), or UV from the Sun (D). The CMB was detected in 1965 and is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.

questions.stem: The age of the universe is estimated at approximately 13.8 billion years. How is this estimate derived?

options.text: By measuring the age of the oldest rocks on Earth
By using the rate of expansion (Hubble constant) to calculate how long ago all matter was together in one point
By counting the number of galaxies in the observable universe
By measuring how long light takes to travel from the Sun to Earth

questions.explanation: By measuring the current rate of expansion (the Hubble constant) and 'running the expansion backwards,' scientists can estimate when all the matter in the universe was concentrated at a single point -- the moment of the Big Bang. This gives an age of approximately 13.8 billion years. The age of Earth's rocks (A) gives Earth's age (4.5 billion years), not the universe's. The number of galaxies (C) does not directly give the age.

questions.stem: A student says: 'The Big Bang was like an explosion that happened at a specific location in space, and the universe expanded outward from that point.' What is wrong with this description?

options.text: Nothing -- this is an accurate description of the Big Bang
The Big Bang was not an explosion at a point in space; it was the rapid expansion of space itself, happening everywhere simultaneously
The Big Bang has not yet been scientifically proven
The Big Bang was an implosion, not an explosion

questions.explanation: A very common misconception is that the Big Bang happened at a specific location. In reality, the Big Bang was the expansion of space itself. It did not happen at a point 'in' space -- space itself was expanding, carrying all matter with it. There is no centre to the expansion. Every point in the universe was the 'point of the Big Bang.' The Big Bang theory is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence (C is wrong).

questions.stem: Two pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory: red shift of galaxies and the cosmic microwave background radiation. A third line of evidence is:

options.text: The abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium) in the universe matches Big Bang predictions
The existence of black holes
The phases of the Moon
The existence of the asteroid belt

questions.explanation: The Big Bang theory predicts that the early universe produced roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium (by mass), with tiny amounts of lithium and deuterium. Observations of the universe's composition closely match these predictions, providing strong supporting evidence. Black holes (B) are predicted by general relativity but are not specific evidence for the Big Bang. The Moon's phases (C) and the asteroid belt (D) are unrelated.

questions.stem: Scientists have discovered that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, not slowing down as originally expected. What is the name given to the mysterious force thought to be driving this acceleration?

options.text: Dark matter
Antimatter
Dark energy
Nuclear energy

questions.explanation: Dark energy is the name given to the unknown force causing the accelerating expansion of the universe. It is estimated to make up about 68% of the total energy content of the universe. Dark matter (A) is a different mystery -- it provides extra gravitational pull that holds galaxies together but does not cause expansion. Antimatter (B) is ordinary matter with opposite charge. Nuclear energy (D) powers stars but does not drive cosmic expansion.
